name: KLOW
used_for: Marketed by research-peptide sellers and clinics as a GLOW variant with KPV added, for skin, inflammation and tissue repair. These uses are promotional claims, not approved indications.
summary: KLOW is a nickname for a four-peptide blend that adds KPV to the GLOW combination of GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500. No approved product contains it, and no combination-specific human study was found in the sources reviewed. A Florida wellness clinic's guide describes such blends as not standardized products and says a blend does not automatically have clinical evidence because its ingredients were researched separately. FDA's compounding page states it has not identified human exposure data on drug products containing KPV. The detailed information is on the pages for KPV, GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500; formulations vary by seller. The combination's side effects are not separately characterized.

side_effects.text: FDA's compounding safety page states it has not identified any human exposure data on drug products containing KPV by any route. This statement concerns a component, not the combination.
side_effects.label: research

internet_claims.claim: Research-peptide sellers describe KLOW as a fixed four-peptide vial combining GHK-Cu, BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV, sold as a research product.
A Florida wellness clinic's guide groups GLOW and KLOW as peptide blends and cautions that they are not standardized products.

research.summary: FDA web page on bulk drug substances for compounding that may present significant safety risks (content dated 22 April 2026, fetched 2026-10-01).
research.finding: FDA lists KPV among withdrawn substances and states it has not identified any human exposure data on drug products containing KPV administered via any route. It lists BPC-157, thymosin beta-4 fragment and GHK-Cu among withdrawn substances with immunogenicity and impurity concerns.

dose.summary: Sellers describe an 80 mg vial of 50 mg GHK-Cu and 10 mg each of KPV, BPC-157 and TB-500, with typical injections of 2 to 4 mg of total blend. No study has tested any dose of this combination, and formulations vary by seller.

items.text: Research-peptide sellers describe KLOW as a fixed four-peptide vial combining GHK-Cu, BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV, sold as a research product.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, describes an 80 mg vial of 50 mg GHK-Cu and 10 mg each of KPV, BPC-157 and TB-500. After adding 3 mL of bacteriostatic water it describes a community titration from about 2 mg of total blend a day, to 4 mg, to 6 mg, then back to 4 mg over 12 weeks.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind, a site that links to sellers, describes 3.2 mg per injection (about 2 mg GHK-Cu and 400 mcg each of KPV, BPC-157 and TB-500) from an 80 mg vial mixed with 3 mL of bacteriostatic water, and says ratios vary by supplier.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer, an education site that says it does not sell peptides, says KLOW is the three-peptide GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 blend at a 5 to 1 to 1 ratio with KPV added, typically sold in 80 mg vials.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptIQ, a site that earns referral fees from partner clinics, lists per-dose ranges of 1 to 2 mg GHK-Cu, 300 to 500 mcg BPC-157, 2 to 2.5 mg TB-500 and 200 to 500 mcg KPV, says supplier ratios vary, and says to work out dose from the label milligrams divided by the water added.
items.label: internet

frequency.summary: Online sources describe one injection a day or Monday to Friday, and one describes 2 to 3 times a week for maintenance. None of this has been studied.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, says the blend is a once-daily injection under the skin.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind, a site that links to sellers, describes injections 5 days a week, Monday through Friday, in the abdomen or thigh.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptIQ, a site that earns referral fees from partner clinics, describes 4 to 5 times a week or daily for acute recovery and 2 to 3 times a week for maintenance, and stresses this is community practice rather than a trial-backed schedule.
items.label: internet

cycle_length.summary: Online sources describe cycles of about 4 to 12 weeks followed by a break. No combination study exists, so these lengths are community convention.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, describes 4 to 6 weeks on and 2 to 4 weeks off as standard, longer cycles of 8 to 12 weeks as reported anecdotally, and says the off period is meant to manage copper build-up from the GHK-Cu part.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind, a site that links to sellers, says protocols typically run 8 to 12 weeks followed by a break.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptIQ, a site that earns referral fees from partner clinics, describes 8 to 12 weeks of loading then time off as common forum practice, not a trial-backed protocol.
items.label: internet

storage_and_handling.summary: Sellers describe mixing the freeze-dried vial with bacteriostatic water, swirling gently, then keeping it in the refrigerator for about 2 to 6 weeks. No stability study of the mixed blend was found, and the sources differ.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, says to swirl rather than shake, to keep the mixed vial at 2 to 8 degrees Celsius and use it within 14 to 28 days, and to avoid repeated freezing and thawing. It lists freezer storage at minus 20 degrees Celsius for the dry powder.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind, a site that links to sellers, says to refrigerate after mixing and use within about a month, avoiding repeated freezing and thawing.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptIQ, a site that earns referral fees from partner clinics, says the mixed vial can be refrigerated for 4 to 6 weeks and that unmixed vials are stable at room temperature.
items.label: internet

mechanism.summary: Sellers describe KLOW as four peptides acting on blood vessel growth, cell movement, inflammation and collagen. This is the sellers' description, not a tested mechanism of the combination, and formulations vary by seller.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, describes GHK-Cu as changing gene activity, KPV as blocking a pro-inflammation switch (NF-kB) in lab models, and BPC-157 and TB-500 as supporting soft-tissue healing and blood vessel growth.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind, a site that links to sellers, says the blend works on healing in different ways at once: blood vessel growth, cell migration, calmer inflammation and more collagen.
items.label: internet

best_documented_effect.summary: No human trial, animal study or registered trial of KLOW was found. Several sources say so themselves, so no effect of the combination is documented.

items.text: A Florida wellness clinic's guide groups GLOW and KLOW as peptide blends and cautions that they are not standardized products.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, says no published clinical trial has evaluated the four-peptide KLOW combination.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind, a site that links to sellers, says the blend has not itself been studied in published clinical trials.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptIQ, a site that earns referral fees from partner clinics, says there is no randomized trial of KLOW as a labeled product.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Regulator warning
side_effect_groups.summary: FDA says it has found no human exposure data on drug products containing KPV, one of the four parts. This is about a component, not the combination.

items.text: FDA's compounding safety page states it has not identified any human exposure data on drug products containing KPV by any route. This statement concerns a component, not the combination.
items.label: research

side_effect_groups.title: Online reports
side_effect_groups.summary: Sellers and guides list injection-site redness and swelling, early fatigue and mild stomach upset. These are not from combination studies.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, lists mild injection-site redness and swelling, a faint blue-green tint, first-week fatigue and short-term digestive changes as common, and headache, lightheadedness, vivid dreams and appetite changes as less common. It says none were measured in controlled blend studies.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Mind, a site that links to sellers, says injection-site redness, swelling or tenderness occurs in an estimated 15 to 20 percent of users and mild stomach symptoms in under 10 percent, without citing a study.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptIQ, a site that earns referral fees from partner clinics, says pitting edema (fluid swelling) is the most commonly reported effect, mainly attributed to the TB-500 part at higher doses, and usually clears in 2 to 4 weeks or with a lower dose.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Warnings
side_effect_groups.summary: One site lists groups told to avoid the blend. This is seller-side advice, not a study result.

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, lists active or recent cancer, copper-metabolism disorders such as Wilson's disease, pregnancy or breastfeeding, and blood thinner use as cautions, and says BPC-157 and TB-500 are banned in tested sport. These reasons concern individual components.
items.label: internet
